questions.question_text: A class records everyone's shoe size. Which of these summary statistics is a measure of spread?

options.text: The range
The mean
options.why: The mean is a measure of centre: it is the total of the sizes shared equally.

options.text: The median
options.why: The median is a measure of centre: it is the middle size once the data is ordered.

options.text: The mode
options.why: The mode is a measure of centre: it is the most common shoe size.

questions.solution_text:
The mean, median and mode each describe a typical shoe size, so they are measures of centre.
The range reports the difference between the largest and smallest size, so it is the measure of spread.

questions.question_text: Which measure of centre is the most common shoe size in a class?

options.text: The mode
The median
options.why: The median is the middle size after sorting, which need not be the most common size.

options.text: The mean
options.why: The mean is the total shared equally, which need not be the most common size.

options.text: The range
options.why: The range is a measure of spread, so it is not a measure of centre at all.

questions.solution_text:
The most frequent value in a dataset is the mode.
The mode is a measure of centre.

questions.question_text: Which list contains exactly the three measures of centre?

options.text: Mean, median, mode
Mean, median, range
options.why: Includes the range, which measures spread, and leaves out the mode.

options.text: Median, mode, range
options.why: Includes the range, which measures spread, and leaves out the mean.

options.text: Mean, mode, maximum
options.why: The maximum is a single data value used to find the range, not a measure of centre.

questions.solution_text:
A measure of centre describes a typical value.
The mean, the median and the mode are the three measures of centre.

questions.question_text: In a class of $26$ students, the difference between the largest and the smallest shoe size is $6$. Which statement about the number $6$ is correct?

options.text: It is the range, a measure of spread.
It is the range, a measure of centre.
options.why: Names the range correctly but classifies a difference between two sizes as a typical size.

options.text: It is the mean, a measure of centre.
options.why: Confuses the difference between the extreme sizes with the total shared equally.

options.text: It is the mode, a measure of centre.
options.why: Confuses the difference between the extreme sizes with the most common size.

questions.solution_text:
The difference between the largest and smallest value is the range.
The range is a measure of spread.

questions.question_text: The shoe sizes of a class are sorted in ascending order and the middle size is $7.5$. Which statement about $7.5$ is correct?

options.text: It is the median, a measure of centre.
It is the median, a measure of spread.
options.why: Names the median correctly but classifies a typical middle value as a description of how spread out the sizes are.

options.text: It is the mode, a measure of centre.
options.why: Confuses the middle size of the ordered list with the most common size, which is the mode.

options.text: It is the mode, a measure of spread.
options.why: Confuses the middle size with the most common size and also classifies that typical value as a measure of spread.

questions.solution_text:
The middle value of the ordered data is the median.
The median is a measure of centre.

questions.question_text: Jai says the range is a measure of centre because it is calculated from the class's shoe sizes. Which response corrects him?

options.text: The range only compares the largest and smallest sizes, so it measures spread.
The range is a measure of centre only once the sizes have been sorted.
options.why: Sorting is needed to find the median, but it does not change what the range measures.

options.text: The range is a measure of centre because it uses every shoe size.
options.why: The range uses only the two extreme sizes, and using the data does not make a statistic a measure of centre.

options.text: The range is neither a measure of centre nor a measure of spread.
options.why: The range is the standard measure of spread for a simple dataset.

questions.solution_text:
Every summary statistic is calculated from the data, so that alone does not make one a measure of centre.
The range reports how far apart the largest and smallest sizes are, so it is a measure of spread.

questions.question_text: Why do statisticians avoid reporting "the average shoe size" without naming a measure?

options.text: "Average" could mean the mean, the median or the mode.
"Average" always means the range, which measures spread.
options.why: The range is a measure of spread and is never referred to as the average.

options.text: "Average" can only be calculated once the data is sorted.
options.why: Sorting is only needed for the median; it is not the reason the word is avoided.

options.text: "Average" is another name for the number of data values.
options.why: The number of data values is $n$, which is not a measure of centre.

questions.solution_text:
There are three measures of centre — the mean, the median and the mode — and they can give three different values for the same dataset.
Naming the measure used says exactly which centre is being reported.
